title: Lavender tincture for mild anxiety
subtitle: A concentrated nervine when a bath is not practical
excerpt: A folk-method lavender tincture made from dried flowers macerated in 40% vodka for four weeks. Traditionally used for mild anxiety and nervous tension. This is a more concentrated preparation than the lavender infusion, useful when a bath is not practical. One to two ml in a little water, up to three times a day.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), lavender entry: documents the nervine use of lavender in infusion and tincture for nervous conditions, tension, and restlessness. BHP (1983) lavender monograph: tincture dosing reference. Culpeper, The English Physician (1652), lavender entry: records use for nervous complaints. EMA HMPC monograph on Lavandulae flos (2012): supports traditional use of lavender flower preparations for anxiety and nervous conditions.

recipe.yieldDescription: Approx. 75 ml tincture (about 37 doses at 2 ml)
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The tincture macerates for 4 weeks before it is ready. Finished tincture stores in a dark glass dropper bottle in a cool dark cupboard for up to 2 years.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Store in an amber glass dropper bottle in a cool dark cupboard. Keeps up to 2 years. Discard if the colour fades noticeably or the smell becomes stale.

glossaryTerms.definition: A liquid herbal preparation made by macerating dried or fresh herb in alcohol. The alcohol draws out and preserves the active compounds; the finished liquid is taken in small measured doses diluted in water.
A herb traditionally used to calm and support the nervous system, easing tension, anxiety, and restlessness without causing significant sedation at standard doses.

projectSchedule.title: Start the maceration
projectSchedule.body: Weigh 15 g of dried lavender flowers into a clean 250 ml glass jar with a tight-fitting lid. Pour over 75 ml of plain 40% vodka, making sure the flowers are fully submerged. Seal the jar, label it with today's date and 'lavender tincture', and put it in a cool dark cupboard.

projectSchedule.title: Check the liquid covers the herb
projectSchedule.body: Open the jar and check the lavender flowers are still submerged. Dried lavender sometimes swells and breaks the surface; if so, top up with a little more vodka. Give the jar a gentle shake, reseal, and return it to the cupboard.

projectSchedule.title: Strain and bottle
projectSchedule.body: Pour the maceration through muslin cloth set over a measuring jug, squeezing the cloth to extract every drop. The tincture should be deep purple-blue and smell strongly of lavender. Use a small funnel to decant into a clean amber glass dropper bottle. Label with the herb, the date, and the alcohol percentage.

content.text: is a concentrated alcohol extract of dried lavender flowers, prepared by macerating them in 40% vodka for four weeks. It is the

preparation western herbalists reach for when they want the full traditional dose of lavender in a practical format: more concentrated than a cup of lavender tea, and useful in situations where a bath is not an option. One to two ml in a small glass of water, up to three times a day, for up to four weeks. The finished
is deep blue-purple with a strong, sweet lavender smell and keeps for up to 2 years in a dark glass bottle.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body:
Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms.

Lavender flowers at culinary and tincture doses have no significant documented drug interactions or safety concerns for most adult readers. The herb has no known cautions at the doses described here.

This preparation contains alcohol (40% ABV vodka). The dose volume is very small (1 to 2 ml), which represents a negligible alcohol intake for most adults. Readers who avoid all alcohol for any reason should consider a lavender infusion instead of this tincture.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding: culinary use of lavender is well tolerated; a tincture is a concentrated preparation with alcohol. Consult a herbalist or your midwife before using this tincture in pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

Paediatric use is not adult-divided-by-half. Consult a herbalist who specialises in children's herbal medicine, or a paediatric doctor, before using any herbal preparation in children under twelve.

When not to use this remedy
See a GP for anxiety that interferes with daily life, comes with panic attacks, intrusive thoughts, or low mood with hopelessness. Herbal calm does not replace assessment.

Readers who avoid all alcohol should use a lavender infusion instead. Consult a herbalist or your midwife before use in pregnancy or while breastfeeding. Do not use in children under twelve without specialist guidance.

items.symptom: Tincture is pale and barely smells of lavender
items.cause: Dried lavender flowers were old or poorly stored before use
items.fix: Start again with fresh dried lavender. It should smell strongly floral and sweet when rubbed between the fingers.

items.symptom: Flowers poking above the vodka surface after a week
items.cause: The flowers swelled as they absorbed the alcohol
items.fix: Top up with a small amount of additional vodka to keep them submerged. Exposed herb above the liquid can develop mould.
